Oral Lesions in a Child

vesicles vs exudate · front of the mouth or back · herpangina vs herpetic gingivostomatitis · the palm and sole rashAre the lesions vesicles or exudate, and do they sit at the front of the mouth or the back?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Sort mouth lesions by type, then site, then the skin: vesicles and ulcers are viral, while tonsillar exudate points to strep, Epstein-Barr virus or adenovirus pharyngitis.
  • Back of the mouth (soft palate, uvula, tonsillar pillars) and no rash: herpangina (coxsackievirus A), supportive care. Front of the mouth with red, swollen gums: herpetic gingivostomatitis (herpes simplex virus type 1), oral acyclovir.
  • Mouth ulcers plus vesicles on the palms and soles: hand-foot-and-mouth disease, supportive care. In all three, watch for dehydration in a child who will not drink.

Coxsackievirus A spreads by the fecal-oral route and peaks in summer and early fall; it causes both herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease, and the skin tells them apart. Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) usually causes gingivostomatitis as its first infection, typically in children, then lies dormant in the trigeminal ganglion and can return as cold sores.

2Urgent risks
Act now
FindingPoints toAction
Refuses all fluids; dry mouth, decreased urine outputDehydration, the main complicationCheck hydration now (mouth, urine output, heart rate); step 4 sets the fluid route.
Fever 5 days or more with red lips or a strawberry tongue, plus conjunctivitis, rash or swollen handsCount the criteria (fever plus 4 of 5); Kawasaki Disease covers the rest.
Thrush with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea and recurrent infectionsSevere combined immunodeficiencyNot simple thrush: look for a T-cell or autoimmune defect.
3Differential
Mouth lesions in a child
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Herpangina (coxsackievirus A)Age 3 to 10, summer or early fall; abrupt fever and sore throat; small gray vesicles that become shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and tonsillar pillars; no rash. Most often the tonsillar pillars and soft palate; the tonsils, uvula or tongue can be involved too.Give fluids and pain control and offer a soft diet without acidic foods; it heals within a week.
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (coxsackievirus A)Young child; painful ulcers on the tongue, cheeks and palate plus a maculopapular, partly vesicular rash on the palms and soles, sometimes the buttocks. Its throat lesions can look just like herpangina; the skin decides.Clinical diagnosis; supportive care and hand hygiene after diaper changes.
Herpetic gingivostomatitis (HSV-1)From 6 months to 5 years, in any season; drools and will not drink; clusters of vesicles at the front (gums, tongue, lips) with red, swollen gums.Give oral acyclovir. In practice: oral antivirals are an option for a first infection, with topical anesthetics for mouth pain.
Recurrent aphthous ulcers (canker sores)Painful shallow ulcers with a gray base and red rim; they come back, often with stress; rarely in the pharynx; usually no fever.Treat with a topical anesthetic or coating; recurrent gastrointestinal symptoms suggest Crohn or celiac disease.
Mouth ulcers with fever every 3 weeks, each bout 3 to 5 days.CBC during a bout; repeat the count a few times each week for 6 weeks or more to confirm.
Oral thrush (oral candidiasis)White plaques that scrape off and may bleed; after antibiotics or corticosteroids, inhaled ones included, or with a weak immune system.Give nystatin suspension; chronic thrush suggests a T-cell or autoimmune defect.
Exudate, not vesicles
DiagnosisDecides itExcluded by
Sore throat and fever without cough; exudate on the tonsils, tender nodes at the front of the neck, petechiae on the palate.Blisters and ulcers in place of exudate.
Adolescent with prolonged fatigue; exudate, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly. No contact sports for a month: the enlarged spleen can rupture.No exudate, nodes or big spleen.
Adenoviral tonsillitisSore throat with fever and cough, at times red eyes (conjunctivitis); exudate but no blisters.Vesicles are not its picture.
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Tongue, lips and gums described as normalNot herpes simplex virus: the front of the mouth is sparedNo acyclovir; supportive care.
Late summer, about to start schoolThe coxsackievirus season, not an exposureUse it only with the site; season alone does not decide.
Runny nose and cough with vesicles at the back of the throatStill herpanginaReassure and observe; no workup.
Blue-white spots on red cheek mucosa with cough, coryza and conjunctivitisWatch for a rash spreading from the face down; Fever and Rash in a Child covers it.
Pause point
5-year-old with gray ulcers on the soft palate and uvula; gums normal Offered as herpetic gingivostomatitis or oral acyclovir Where are the lesions, and are the gums red and swollen? → Back of the mouth, gums spared: herpangina, supportive care
Young child with mouth ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles Offered as herpangina Is the skin involved? → Hand-foot-and-mouth disease: supportive care
Toddler with mouth ulcers and fever every 3 weeks, well between Offered as aphthous ulcers or a viral illness Do the bouts come back on a fixed cycle, with fever? → Cyclic neutropenia: CBC during a bout

Site first, then the skin, then the season or the 3-week cycle.

Practice
  1. 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with throat pain, 1 mm vesicles on the tonsillar pillars and gray shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula, tongue and lips and buccal mucosa spared, no rash → Coxsackievirus A → herpangina
  2. 2 yo with fever, drooling and refusal to drink; clusters of vesicles on the tongue, lips and gums, which are red and swollen → Herpetic gingivostomatitis → oral acyclovir
  3. 3 yo with fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles → Hand-foot-and-mouth disease → supportive care
  4. 5 yo with posterior oral vesicles and ulcers, drinking less but with moist mucous membranes and normal vital signs → Cold non-acidic fluids with analgesia → herpangina resolves within a week
  5. 8 yo with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes, without cough or oral vesicles → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → rapid antigen testing before treating
  6. 16 yo with 2 weeks of fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly → Epstein-Barr virus infection → avoid contact sports
  7. 5 yo with gray vesicles and ulcers confined to the soft palate and uvula, no rash, well hydrated → Oral acyclovir → herpangina is an enteroviral illness, not a herpesvirus one
  8. 4 yo with herpangina now refusing all fluids, with dry mucous membranes and no urine output for 10 hours; HR 160, cool hands, capillary refill 4 seconds → Intravenous rehydration → dehydration is the principal complication
  9. 5 yo in late summer with abrupt fever and sore throat; gray vesicles and shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and tonsillar pillars; gums, lips and tongue normal; no rash → Herpangina → coxsackievirus A; supportive care
Pearls Between herpangina and gingivostomatitis, the front of the mouth (gums, tongue, lips) is herpes; the back (soft palate, uvula, tonsillar pillars) is coxsackie – both diseases otherwise present with fever, sore throat and a miserable child · Vesicles and ulcers exclude exudate-producing pathogens wholesale: strep, Epstein-Barr virus and adenovirus make exudate, not blisters · Herpangina has no rash; hand-foot-and-mouth does – same virus family, separated by the skin · Red swollen gingiva is the HSV signature, and its absence is as informative as any positive finding · Starting the fall term in two weeks is dating the season, not describing an exposure · Hand hygiene, above all around diaper changes, is the public-health answer
Pairs with Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the exudative pharyngitis fork and the Centor rule; this brief covers vesicular lesions. Ask: are the lesions exudate or vesicles, and are they front or back? Fever and Rash in a Child covers the other rashes with fever and points here for hand-foot-and-mouth disease.
Transferable rule When two diseases share a lesion type, the discriminating attribute is usually anatomical, not clinical. Ask where the lesions are before asking what they are. Treat a stated spared structure as an active exclusion, not as background.
Unchecked attributeHerpes simplex virus: oral vesicles in a child bring HSV to mind, but HSV sits at the front of the mouth; when the gums, tongue and lips are spared and the gums are not swollen, it does not fit.
Class-vs-memberAdenovirus: a common cause of pediatric fever with sore throat, but it produces exudative tonsillitis, not vesicles or ulcers.
Class-vs-memberStreptococcus pyogenes: exudate with tender anterior nodes; vesicles and ulcers argue against it.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus: needs exudate, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and adolescent age, none of which herpangina brings.
